Knee Pain While Climbing Stairs? Understanding What Your Knees May Be Telling You

Dr. Surabhi Vaidya · BAMS, MD (Ayurveda) Charak Health Solutions · Raymond TenX Habitat, Thane West
📅 November 2026 ⏱ 5 min read 🏷 Knee Health

Does climbing a flight of stairs make your knees hurt? Do you feel discomfort when getting up from a chair or walking downstairs?

For many people, knee pain begins as a minor inconvenience. They avoid a few stairs, take extra support while walking, or assume the discomfort is simply because of age.

But knee pain during everyday movement can have several causes.

Pain while climbing stairs does not automatically mean arthritis, permanent joint damage, or the need for surgery. Understanding the possible cause is the first step towards managing it appropriately.

Why do knees hurt while climbing stairs?

Your knee joint helps support your body weight while walking, bending, standing and climbing stairs.

Going up or down stairs places different demands on the kneecap, surrounding muscles and other joint structures compared with walking on flat ground.

If one of these structures is irritated or not functioning comfortably, stair climbing may trigger pain.

1. Knee osteoarthritis

Osteoarthritis involves changes in cartilage, bone and other joint tissues.

Common symptoms include:

  • Pain during walking or climbing stairs
  • Stiffness after resting
  • Occasional swelling
  • Difficulty getting up from a chair

Osteoarthritis becomes more common with increasing age, but not everyone experiencing knee pain has arthritis.

2. Patellofemoral pain

This condition typically causes discomfort around or behind the kneecap.

Pain may increase while climbing stairs, squatting, running or sitting for a long time with bent knees.

It can occur in younger and older adults.

3. Reduced muscle strength

The muscles around your thighs and hips support movement and help control knee loading.

Reduced strength or endurance can make activities like stair climbing more uncomfortable.

However, muscle weakness should not be assumed to be the cause without proper assessment.

4. Meniscus or ligament injuries

Injuries to structures inside or around the knee can lead to pain, swelling, instability or difficulty bending.

Symptoms following a fall, twisting injury or sudden movement should be evaluated appropriately.

What should you do when your knees hurt on stairs?

The right approach depends on the reason for your pain.

For mild discomfort without an injury or warning signs, some general precautions may help:

  • Reduce activities that repeatedly aggravate the pain: You may temporarily need to limit frequent stair climbing or deep squatting.
  • Remain comfortably active: Completely stopping movement is usually unnecessary. Choose activities that do not significantly worsen your symptoms.
  • Pay attention to swelling: A cold pack wrapped in a towel may provide temporary comfort.
  • Consider guided strengthening: Appropriate exercises may help improve movement and function, but they should be selected according to your condition.
  • Avoid forcing painful stretches: Avoid following the same exercise routine recommended to someone with a different knee problem.

When should you consult a healthcare professional?

Consider an assessment if your knee pain:

  • Continues beyond a few weeks
  • Repeatedly limits walking or climbing stairs
  • Comes with recurring swelling or stiffness
  • Interferes with sleep or everyday activities
  • Is getting progressively worse
⚠️ Urgent Medical Warning Signs

Seek urgent medical care if:

  • Your knee becomes severely swollen, locked, or visibly deformed
  • You cannot bear any weight on the leg after an injury or fall
  • The joint becomes hot, red, and swollen with fever or systemic chills
These signs may indicate an acute infection, severe fracture, or major ligament tear requiring emergency hospital assessment.

Can knee pain improve without surgery?

Many knee conditions can be managed with non-surgical approaches, depending on their cause and severity.

These may include suitable exercise, lifestyle adjustments, weight management when relevant, and condition-specific medical care.

Surgery is considered in selected circumstances, particularly when significant symptoms and functional limitations persist despite appropriate treatment.

There is no single treatment that suits every person with knee pain.
